notes.b: Cost-benefit analysis compares the expected costs of a decision with its expected benefits, so the business can judge whether the decision is worth making.
points: It makes the business weigh the downside of a decision as well as the upside, which guards against decisions based only on optimism.
It can be applied to any major decision, such as opening a new site, buying a rival or launching a product.
Its result depends on forecasts, so it is only as good as the figures entered.

notes.b: The method follows five stages, which should be completed in order.
points: Identify the decision and the alternatives being compared.
List all costs and benefits, both financial and non-financial, for the firm and for stakeholders such as staff, customers and the local community.
Quantify each item where possible by giving it a money value.
Compare total benefits with total costs over the period chosen.
Decide, and justify the decision by reference to the comparison and to any non-financial factors.

notes.b: Items in the analysis fall into two groups, and each needs a different kind of treatment.
points: Tangible items can be measured in money, such as sales revenue, equipment cost and rent.
Intangible items are real but hard to measure in money, such as brand reputation, staff morale and customer goodwill.
Intangible items should still be listed, because leaving them out can distort the decision.
A common approach is to estimate a money value for an intangible item, or to record it as a qualitative factor in the final recommendation.

notes.b: Two further factors change the comparison: what is given up by choosing an option, and when costs and benefits arise.
points: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made, such as using the cash to fund marketing instead.
Start-up costs such as a fit-out usually arise before benefits, so the timing of costs and benefits affects the comparison.
A short-term view looks at the first year's cash position, while a longer view counts benefits over several years.

notes.h: Worked example: investment figures and yearly results
notes.b: The example uses invented sample figures for a bakery deciding whether to open a second shop in Galway. Sales are held at the same level in each year after the opening.
points: Sample figures, one-off costs in year 1: fit-out and equipment €180,000, initial marketing €15,000.
Sample figures, annual running costs: rent €36,000, wages €60,000, and ingredients and packaging €90,000, which is 30 per cent of sales.
Sample figures, annual sales from the Galway shop: €300,000 in each year.
Sample figures, year 2: benefits €300,000, costs €186,000 (€36,000 + €60,000 + €90,000), net result €114,000.
Sample figures, year 3: benefits €300,000, costs €186,000, net result €114,000.
Sample figures, three-year total: minus €81,000 + €114,000 + €114,000, which is €147,000.

notes.h: Worked example: payback, sensitivity and decision
notes.b: The remaining steps test how quickly the outlay is recovered and whether the result survives a fall in sales.
points: Sample figures, payback: the cumulative position moves from minus €81,000 at the end of year 1 to €33,000 at the end of year 2, so the outlay is recovered in year 2.
Sample figures, sensitivity: if sales fall 10 per cent to €270,000 a year and ingredients fall to €81,000, the three-year total is €84,000, which is still positive.
Non-financial benefits include new jobs in Galway, a stronger brand presence in the west and management experience for staff.
Non-financial costs include the management time the owners must give to the Galway project, which may slow the development of the existing Limerick shop.

Recommendation: proceed, because the three-year result stays positive even if sales fall 10 per cent, and the outlay is recovered in year 2, provided a staffing plan limits disruption to the Limerick shop.

notes.b: The method is a useful guide, but its result has limits that the decision-maker should state.
points: Results depend on forecasts, which can be wrong, particularly sales forecasts for a new location.
Intangible effects are hard to value, so the final figure may leave out factors that matter most to stakeholders.
The choice of time period can change the answer: a short period may hide benefits that arrive later, while a long one relies on distant forecasts.
The result shows a net gain but not the risk of failure or the cash the firm must find before benefits start to arrive.
The analysis takes time and money to prepare, which may not be worthwhile for small, low-risk decisions.

keyTerms.definition: A method of comparing the expected costs of a decision with its expected benefits to decide whether it is worthwhile.
A cost or benefit that can be measured and expressed in money.
A cost or benefit that is real but difficult to measure in money, such as reputation or staff morale.
The value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made.
The time taken for cumulative net benefits to recover the initial outlay.
A cost that does not involve a direct outflow of money, such as lost staff time or disruption to existing customers.
Any individual or group affected by a business decision, such as staff, customers, suppliers or the local community.
Total benefits minus total costs for a decision over a stated period.

Main weakness of the comparison method

questions.prompt: A hotel group is deciding whether to buy a rival hotel in Kerry. Identify the main financial and non-financial costs and benefits, explain how the analysis would be quantified, and recommend a decision.
questions.model: Financial costs: the purchase price, including any premium over market value, refurbishment and integration costs, and interest on borrowed funds. Financial benefits: extra room revenue, savings from shared purchasing and any rise in occupancy. Non-financial costs: uncertainty for the staff of both hotels, a possible competition review and a clash of brands. Non-financial benefits: a larger presence in Kerry and a stronger position with tour operators. Quantification: estimate each money item over several years, value intangible factors where possible, then compare total benefits with total costs and calculate the net benefit. Recommendation: proceed only if the net benefit stays positive when occupancy is lower than forecast and the regulatory review is cleared.

questions.prompt: Explain the term opportunity cost and give one example relevant to a business choosing between two expansion projects.
questions.model: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made. If the business commits its funds to a new shop, the opportunity cost is the output and profit the production line it did not build would have generated.
